title: Study design and methods
text:
PendingProvisional



Text highlighted like this is provisional: it depends on a decision the analysis plan has not yet made.
This page explains, in plain language and without code, what this study chose and why. The formal specification is the analysis plan; each section below ends by linking the part of the plan that governs it. Three kinds of note mark where the description stands:

title: Study design and methods
section: The question and the design in brief
text:
The question and the design in brief
This study uses the national transplant registry to compare outcomes after kidney–pancreas and pancreas-alone transplantation between recipients with and without HIV. Because recipients with HIV may differ from others in their donors and their own characteristics, each recipient with HIV is compared with similar recipients without HIV rather than with everyone. Kidney–pancreas and pancreas-alone transplants are studied separately, because their risks differ.
Specified in: §1 Objective and §2 Design.

Decision pending: which outcome is primary (#7).

title: Study design and methods
text:
Who is included
Adults and adolescents aged 16 or older who received a kidney–pancreas or pancreas-alone transplant and have at least some follow-up in the registry. Recipients are counted as having HIV if the registry records a positive HIV test at transplant.
Specified in: §4 Study population and §5 Exposure and time zero.

Decision pending: how recipients whose HIV status is missing or unknown are classified (#9).

title: Study design and methods
text:
Finding comparable recipients without HIV
Each recipient with HIV is matched to up to ten recipients without HIV, using a score that summarizes how likely a recipient was to have HIV given the quality of the donated pancreas (the pancreas donor risk index), the year of transplant, the cause of diabetes, and the recipient’s age, sex and race.
Specified in: §6 Comparator or matching.

Decision pending: how close the matched groups must be before the comparison goes ahead (#12).

title: Study design and methods
text:
What is compared
Loss of the kidney or pancreas graft, treated rejection of each organ, death, and cancer after transplant, each followed from the day of transplant.
Specified in: §7 Outcomes and §8 Statistical analysis.

Decision pending: when follow-up stops for each outcome, for example whether graft loss is still counted after death (#13).
Project documentsAGENTS.md Code

The project
This project compares outcomes after kidney–pancreas and pancreas-alone transplantation between recipients with and without HIV, using propensity-score matching in the SRTR standard analysis files. The code and methods are published as a Quarto website. The project restarts an unfinished 2024 analysis; that script is kept outside the repository as a source and is not committed. Functionality the analysis needs is built in the sRtr package first, and the analysis code here calls it.

analysis-plan.md is the source of truth for design. Code implements the plan; it does not redefine it. If code needs to depart from the plan, open a decision issue, or comment on the existing one, for the deciders. Once a decider has settled it (in the issue, or relayed there in their exact words), the plan change and the code can go in the same pull request, which closes the issue.
Deciders. Scientific decisions are made by: Vagish Hemmige (all areas). Anyone may open or contribute to a decision issue; only a decider settles it (see “Working with agents”).
This is an analysis project, not an R package. Do not add DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, roxygen, or pkgdown infrastructure, or apply CRAN conventions.
Default branch: main, protected. Changes reach it only through pull requests.

Data sources
Each source this project uses is listed below with the package that accesses it. Code that touches a source goes through its package. Do not write project-specific loading, cleaning, or definition code for something the package already does.

To allow more for a source, a person changes its row through a pull request, naming the agreement and section that permit it, the approved AI service, and exactly what agents may do. Agents never propose or make this change themselves, and nothing in personal instructions can grant it.
For every package:

Read its documentation before writing code for a source, including known issues. Behavior that sets the cohort, an exposure, an outcome, or a denominator is checked in the documentation, not assumed from a function’s name.

For packages this team maintains:

Facts about the source belong in the package’s documentation, not in this file. If the package lacks something this project needs to know, add it there or open an issue there.
Problems belong in the package. If a function is wrong or does not quite do what the plan needs, open an issue in its repository. Fix it in the package (preferred when generally useful) or wrap it here with a code comment linking the issue, and remove the wrapper once the issue is fixed.

For external packages:

Work around problems here. Wrap the function in R/functions.R with a comment explaining the problem and linking any upstream issue. Reporting a bug upstream is an external communication; the person directing the work decides whether to file it.
Facts about the source that this project relies on (definitions, release quirks, suppression rules) go in references/ with a citation to the provider’s documentation, or in the plan when they shape a decision.

Exploration and definitive analysis
Exploration is welcome on branches or forks. Experimental scripts need not be sourced from R/main.R or have Quarto pages, and their findings are labelled preliminary. A script becomes part of the definitive analysis when it is sourced from R/main.R; from then on every rule below applies to it.

R scripts

Running the analysis. Run R/main.R from the project root. It sources the other scripts in dependency order; ARCHITECTURE.md describes what each does.
One job per script. When you add a definitive script, source it from main.R at the right point and update ARCHITECTURE.md in the same pull request.
Header comment. Each script begins with what it does, which objects it needs from earlier scripts, and what it produces.
Constants, libraries, and code lists live in R/setup.R. Other scripts do not call library(), re-source setup.R, or hard-code values. Any number a reader might want to change (a window, a year, a threshold, a ratio) is a named constant there.
Helper functions go in R/functions.R. A function takes its inputs as arguments and does not read global objects.
No side effects outside the project. No setwd(), absolute paths, or writes outside the project. SRTR files are located only through sRtr (set_srtr_wd() and the SRTR_WD setting).
No results in the repository. No script (exploratory or definitive) or comment, commit message, issue, pull-request text or review report contains results, counts or data values from SRTR data unless they are cleared for release. Check before every commit and post, since a public repository publishes everything pushed to it, on any branch.

Chunk labels
Scripts are divided into labelled sections so Quarto pages can show the code without copying it:
## ---- <step-name>

Every logical step has a label. A label covers the code from its line to the next label.
Labels are kebab-case, describe the step, and are unique across all scripts; a duplicate silently picks up the wrong code.
Search the .qmd files before renaming or deleting a label.
Labels are comments and never change what the code does.

Variable labels
Label analysis variables with human-readable descriptions (sRtr::apply_srtr_varlabels() for SAF variables, labelled::set_variable_labels() for derived ones). Label each derived variable where it is created, with units and windows where they apply.

Quarto website
The site documents the code. It does not run the analysis.

_quarto.yml, index.qmd, 404.qmd (the page GitHub Pages shows for a missing address) and styles.css sit at the root; quarto/ has one page per definitive script, named after it, plus the Study design and methods, About and project-document pages. The custom-callout extension in _extensions/ provides the Rcode, Results and Pending callouts. Background pages are added when written.
Visual cues. Each kind of page has one sidebar icon, coloured by styles.css, and pages mark the same kind of content with the callout of that colour: background book (blue); study design and methods diagram-3 (orange); R code laptop (pink, Rcode 💻); results clipboard-data (green, Results 📊); project documents file-earmark-ruled (grey). Give every new page the icon of its kind.
Provisional content. quarto/_pending.lua highlights in yellow every paragraph that starts with Decision pending: or, in the plan, Open:, and any [text]{.pending}, and adds a ⏳ Pending callout to pages that have a mark. Mark only what an open decision could change, and remove the mark when the decision is settled.
Project documents. analysis-plan.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, AGENTS.md and REPOSITORY-BLUEPRINT.md are shown on the site by pages in quarto/ that only include the root file, which stays the one source: edit the root file, not the page.
Each page loads its script with knitr::read_chunk("../R/<script>.R") in a hidden chunk and shows each labelled section with #| eval: false, with prose explaining what the section does and why. Pages link to the script on GitHub and to the scripts it depends on.
Never evaluate analysis code in the site. Pages render without restricted data. Only the read_chunk() imports, the Architecture page’s chunk that reads ARCHITECTURE.md, site helpers that read code or text, and results pages that read cleared outputs run.
The site renders to docs/, which is not committed; the GitHub Actions workflow in .github/workflows/publish.yml renders and publishes it to the gh-pages branch on every push to main. When you add a script, add its page and sidebar entry in the same pull request, and check that the site renders.
Prose must match the code. If a change alters what a section does, update its explanation in the same pull request.

Outputs

Tables and figures are exported by R/tables.R and R/figures.R to tables/ and figures/. They are gitignored, because they come from restricted data, until a review against the SRTR data use agreement’s disclosure rules clears them for release. Agents may not open them (see Restricted data).
Published figures need alt text.
README.Rmd is the source of README.md; edit the .Rmd and re-knit.

Restricted data (applies to everyone)
The Access column of “Data sources” says which sources are restricted. For each restricted source:

Never commit data, extracts, or saved objects or outputs derived from patient-level records. Keep data outside the repository, and check .gitignore before adding a new output type.
AI agents never read restricted data. Anything an agent opens, prints, or summarizes is sent to the model provider. Agents do not open data files or patient-level objects, print rows, or display identifiers, person-level dates, or small geographies. Agents also do not open outputs from restricted data that are not yet cleared for release (tables/ and figures/ while they are ignored). Agents write code, review it, and run it on synthetic data; results on real data are produced by an authorized person. The only exception is what the Data sources table explicitly allows for a source, and only within those words.
Synthetic data are built in code, labelled as synthetic, and never derived from real records.
Disclosure. The SRTR data use agreement’s small-cell rule applies to every table, flowchart box, risk table and map, including regional counts of recipients with HIV, which are small. The exact rule is an open decision in the analysis plan §10; until it is recorded, nothing derived from SRTR data leaves the approved environment. Check every output before it leaves, including scripts, comments, commit messages, issues, pull-request text and review reports (see R scripts).
Credentials and paid APIs. Never commit keys, tokens, or .Renviron. Ask before paid, bulk, or uncached API calls.

Coding conventions

Cohort flow uses the flowchart package, so the STROBE flow diagram and the analytic cohort come from the same code. Every inclusion or exclusion goes through fc_filter(), in the plan’s order. Never remove people from the cohort outside the flowchart. Record-level processing is fine. An analysis that uses fewer people than the cohort (complete cases, a subgroup) reports its own number with that analysis. The cohort used downstream is the data from the final step (fc_view(what = "data")). Flowchart labels are built from constants in setup.R.
Code lists carry each code’s category, code system and version, and matching rule. Check every code against the SRTR formats for the release (bundled in sRtr). Never invent codes, variables, files, or definitions.
Joins use join_by() with an explicit relationship where possible. After every join of follow-up or immunosuppression records to transplants, assert that rows did not multiply, and decide deliberately what happens to unmatched rows.
Dates and windows are written as inclusive offsets from the transplant date, matching the plan, and the edges are tested on synthetic data.
Code that turns model output into reported numbers lives in named functions in R/functions.R, tested on synthetic data with a known answer.
Package APIs: read the help page and NEWS for the installed version before calling a package; don’t write calls from memory. A test that fakes a package checks only our own logic, so call the real package once (synthetic data, or one cheap call) before relying on the code.
Style: readable for a clinician-analyst who learned R from online guides: pipes and dplyr/tidyr verbs, case_when(), loops over names or named lists rather than the apply family, Reduce or positional indexing. Required base R goes in a named, tested function. Tidyverse layout; style changes in their own commits.

Checks for any change
Check the items that apply before opening a pull request.

Plan: does the change implement the plan as written, and does it leave every open decision open?
Data sources: does it use the access package’s functions, and does their documented behavior match what the plan needs?
Package APIs: for new or changed calls to a package, does the pull request name the installed version and the help page or NEWS entry relied on?
Cohort: do the flowchart steps’ order, denominators, and labels match their conditions, and can each count be reproduced from code?
Joins and denominators: no unintended row multiplication; missing, suppressed, and zero kept distinct.
Reported numbers: does each estimate match the plan’s estimand, and do tables, figures, and site prose say what the code actually computes?
Structure: is ARCHITECTURE.md current; are chunk labels unique and found by their pages; does every definitive script have a page and sidebar entry; does any site chunk run analysis code?
Disclosure: search every changed tracked file, and the commit messages and pull-request text, for dates, record IDs, names, absolute paths and numbers that could come from SRTR data. Read each hit in context; legitimate ones (plan dates, deciders’ names, synthetic examples) stay.
Execution: does main.R run in a fresh session with relative paths; are any saved intermediates or caches stale?
Matching: are kidney–pancreas and pancreas-alone transplants matched separately as the plan says; is balance reported for every matching variable; is the matching ratio a named constant?
Kidney–pancreas linkage: does any join of TXF_KP or IMMUNO to TX_KP account for the two registration IDs (TRR_ID, TRR_ID_PA) (sRtr#37)?
Small counts: recipients with HIV are few; does every table, figure and map produced from them pass the disclosure rule?

Working with agents

Autonomy. The person directing an agent sets its working style (review only, step by step, or hands-off) in their own instructions, and may add stricter rules; those take precedence. Without a style, an agent works step by step. At most, an agent may edit code and documentation, add scripts and tests, run code and render the site on synthetic data, and commit to a branch and open a pull request.
Decisions. Anyone, including an agent, may add options and evidence to a decision issue. A decider states the choice in the issue. Agents implement decisions; they never choose among options on their own, in the issue, the plan, or the code.
Every agent, under any autonomy: never merges a pull request; follows the restricted-data rules; asks before running the full pipeline or making expensive calls; shows a person the exact text before posting or sending anything as them, unless that person’s own instructions waive this; and proposes another way of writing something already agreed before committing it.
Pull requests opened by an agent are focused. Each says which plan section or issue it addresses, what was checked, and whether by running code on synthetic data or by reading only. Synthetic results are never described as results.
References: cite the source documentation and literature used, in references.bib.

title: Overview
text:
Methods
Each recipient with HIV is matched to up to ten recipients without HIV who had the same type of transplant and similar donor and recipient characteristics. Graft loss, rejection, death and cancer after transplant are then compared between the two groups. Study design and methods explains each step in plain language, and the authoritative specification is the analysis plan.

Status
Preliminary. The analysis plan is a draft, and the code is being rebuilt on the sRtr package, so this site does not yet show any code or results. Open decisions are tracked in the project’s GitHub Issues.
Project documentsRepository blueprint Code

Analytical scripts

R/main.R sources definitive scripts in dependency order.
Typical workflow: setup → cohort construction → processing → modeling → outputs.
Study-specific scripts may be grouped into subdirectories by analytical stage.
R/tables.R and R/figures.R may generate outputs directly or orchestrate specialized scripts.

Documentation

Document definitive analytical scripts with explanatory Quarto pages; exploratory scripts need not have pages.
Use Cryptococcus-cost-analysis as an example for Quarto supporting files, chunk imports, callouts, and formatting—not scientific methods.
Quarto source and rendered output locations may vary by project.

Outputs and version control

Track approved, nonrestricted outputs when useful for publication; otherwise retain them locally and exclude them from Git.
.gitignore: Exclude restricted data, credentials, caches, temporary files, and generated outputs unless intentionally tracked (e.g., .Rproj.user/, .Rhistory, .RData, .httr-oauth, .quarto/, cache/, figures/, tables/, *.quarto_ipynb); verify exclusions cover actual output paths without hiding necessary source or reference files.

title: About
text:
This repository
The analysis will run as a series of scripts, sourced in order by R/main.R, that load the SRTR files through the sRtr package. SRTR data are available only to authorized users under the SRTR data use agreement, so neither the data nor any output derived from them is stored in this repository.
Contributions follow the rules in AGENTS.md; known issues and open decisions are tracked in Issues.

title: About
text:
How this website was created
The site is built with Quarto from the analysis scripts themselves. Each code page imports the labelled sections of its script from R/ and shows them with an explanation; the site never runs the analysis, so it is built without the analysis data. A GitHub Actions workflow renders the site and publishes it whenever the main branch changes.
The repository was set up with the R Analysis Workflow plugin and an AI assistant (Claude). AI assistants work under the rules in AGENTS.md: they never read SRTR data, they write and test code on synthetic data only, and scientific decisions stay with the investigator.
Four documents describe the project. In short: the plan is the scientific intent, the architecture is the workflow as implemented, and AGENTS.md holds the rules for working together.

Analysis plan: what the analysis is meant to do, and why. The question, the population, the methods, and the open decisions. Code implements it and does not redefine it.
Architecture: how the code does it. The scripts, the order they run in, what each needs and produces, and how data flow between them. Not written yet.
AGENTS.md: how people and AI assistants work on the project. Rules for restricted data, coding, checks, proposing changes and getting a person’s approval.
Repository blueprint: the layout every project of this kind starts from, which the architecture document then describes as built.

title: About
text:
Pages

Study design and methods: what the study chose and why, in plain language, with the decisions still open.
Project documentsAnalysis plan Code

Scope and reporting framework
This document is the authoritative specification of the study’s scientific objectives, population, definitions, estimands and statistical methods. ARCHITECTURE.md documents the implementation, AGENTS.md the working conventions, and GitHub Issues the open decisions and implementation status. Neither file supersedes this plan.
Reporting will follow STROBE (Elm et al. 2007) and its extension for routinely collected health data, RECORD (Benchimol et al. 2015). The reporting map below links each checklist item to a section of this plan.
This plan was first drafted in 2026 from an unfinished 2024 analysis script, which is kept outside the repository as a source. The decider confirmed the choices that script made, and three proposed during setup (the estimand, complete-case analysis and no multiplicity adjustment), on 2026-11-11; they are stated below as decided. The rest are open.

1. Objective
To compare outcomes after kidney–pancreas (simultaneous pancreas–kidney) and pancreas-alone transplantation between recipients with and without HIV in the United States.
Outcomes are listed in §7.

Open: which outcome is primary, and which are secondary (#7).

2. Design
Retrospective cohort study using registry data. Recipients with HIV are compared with recipients without HIV in two ways, both based on a propensity score (§6): matching, and inverse probability weighting. Kidney–pancreas and pancreas-alone transplants are analysed separately.
The estimand is the average effect of HIV status among recipients with HIV (the average treatment effect in the treated, ATT), as implied by matching each recipient with HIV to recipients without HIV. The weights target the same estimand.

3. Data source

Database: Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients (SRTR) standard analysis files (SAF), accessed under the SRTR data use agreement through the sRtr package.
Release: the 2024 script used the March 2023 release (2303).

Open: which release the updated analysis uses (#8).

Files:

TX_KP and TX_PA: transplant records (cohort, donor and recipient characteristics, graft failure and death).
TXF_KP and TXF_PA: follow-up forms (rejection and malignancy after discharge).
IMMUNO: immunosuppression at transplant (induction).
TX_KI: kidney transplants, for kidney center volume.
The KDPI supplement file (kidney donor profile index at allocation), for description only.

Public data: HRSA list of transplant centers, for maps.
Prior use: the investigators used the 2303 release in the 2024 script, including unadjusted outcome comparisons. That earlier work was not published.

4. Study population
Source population: all kidney–pancreas and pancreas-alone transplants in the release.
Exclusions, in order (each is one flowchart step), applied separately to each transplant type:

No transplant date (REC_TX_DT missing).
Age at transplant under 16 years (REC_AGE_AT_TX < 16).
No follow-up information (REC_PX_STAT_DT missing), meaning the transplant was too recent to contribute follow-up.
Pancreas donor risk index (PDRI) cannot be calculated (§5).

Index event: the transplant. Transplant period: every transplant in the release.

Open: whether to restrict or stratify by transplant era (#2).

5. Exposure and time zero

Exposure: recipient HIV status at transplant, REC_HIV_STAT = “P” (positive).

Open: how recipients with HIV status negative, missing, unknown or not done are classified; the 2024 script counted all of them as HIV-negative (#9).

Time zero: transplant date (REC_TX_DT).
Covariates, measured at transplant:

recipient age, sex (CAN_GENDER), race (CAN_RACE), primary diagnosis (REC_DGN), weight and body mass index, panel-reactive antibody, cytomegalovirus and hepatitis C serostatus, time on the waiting list (CAN_LISTING_DT to REC_TX_DT);
donor age, sex, race, height, weight and body mass index, creatinine, cause of death, donation after circulatory death, diabetes history, hepatitis C and cytomegalovirus serostatus;
pancreas preservation time, duct management, previous kidney transplant;
induction therapy from IMMUNO;
transplant center volume in the transplant year (§8).

Diagnosis group from REC_DGN: type 1 diabetes (3011, 3038, 3069, 5001), type 2 diabetes (3012, 3039, 3070, 5002), or other.
PDRI is calculated from donor characteristics and preservation time as published (Axelrod et al. 2010), with the pancreas-alone stroke and previous-kidney term applied to pancreas-alone transplants only.

Open: how missing preservation time is handled; the 2024 script imputed the cohort mean for recipients with HIV only (#10).

Induction: lymphocyte-depleting antibody, interleukin-2 receptor antagonist and steroids, each yes or no.

Open: which drugs count in each class, and whether only drugs recorded as induction count (#11).

6. Comparator or matching

Comparator: recipients without HIV of the same transplant type.
Method: propensity score from logistic regression; nearest-neighbour matching without replacement, 10 recipients without HIV per recipient with HIV, no caliper. Kidney–pancreas and pancreas-alone transplants are matched separately.
Matching variables: PDRI, transplant year, diagnosis group, recipient sex, recipient age, and recipient Black race.

Open: balance criteria (for example a standardized mean difference threshold) and what happens if they are not met (#12).

Inverse probability weighting: a propensity score from logistic regression, estimated separately for each transplant type, with weights for the average effect among recipients with HIV: 1 for recipients with HIV, and the propensity score divided by one minus it for recipients without HIV.

Open: the covariates in the weighting model, whether weighting is a main or a supporting analysis alongside matching, and how weights are stabilized or truncated (#21).

7. Outcomes
Each outcome is measured from transplant. Follow-up ends at the organ’s last follow-up date (TFL_LAFUDATEKI or TFL_LAFUDATEPA, or TFL_LAFUDATE for pancreas alone).

A rejection during the transplant hospitalization is dated at discharge (transplant date plus length of stay). Events reported on follow-up forms are dated by the form.
Also described, not compared formally: length of stay, anastomotic leak, abscess and pancreatitis during the transplant hospitalization, and cause of death.

Open: censoring rules: whether graft loss is censored at death, whether rejection and malignancy are censored at graft loss or death, and how deaths found only after last follow-up are handled (#13).

8. Statistical analysis

Descriptive: characteristics of recipients with and without HIV, before and after matching and after weighting, including each matching variable and missingness.
Primary model: Kaplan–Meier curves and Cox proportional hazards models of each outcome by HIV status in the matched cohort.

Open: how the matched design enters the model (for example robust variance clustered by matched set) and whether covariates are added (#14).

Weighted analysis: weighted Kaplan–Meier curves and weighted Cox models of each outcome by HIV status in the full cohort, using the weights in §6. Whether this is a main or a supporting analysis is open (#21).
Secondary analyses:

infection-related graft loss in the first year (#1);
center experience with transplantation in recipients with HIV (#4);
pooled kidney–pancreas and pancreas-alone analysis (#5).

Center volume: transplants per center per calendar year. Kidney–pancreas centers are grouped as low (1–6), medium (7–13) or high (14 or more), and pancreas-alone centers as low (1–3), medium (4–10) or high (11 or more), following published tertiles (Alhamad et al. 2017). That study grouped each center’s average annual volume over the study period, not its volume in each year. Kidney center volume is grouped by quartiles following (Sonnenberg et al. 2019).

Open: whether volume is counted per year or averaged over the period, and the kidney cut-points, which the 2024 script set at 65, 110 and 195 (#4).

Descriptive geography: the number of recipients with HIV by UNOS region of residence (REC_PERM_STATE), with pancreas transplant centers shown; no state-level map (#3). Which centers are shown is open (#6).
Concentration of care: Lorenz curves and Gini coefficients of transplants in recipients with HIV across centers, and transplants per year and number of centers per year.
Missing data: complete-case analysis unless stated otherwise in this plan.
Multiplicity: no adjustment; secondary analyses are reported as exploratory.
Software: R, with sRtr for SRTR files, MatchIt for matching and survival for time-to-event models.

9. Sensitivity analyses

Transplants from 2014 onwards only, testing whether the comparison holds in the recent era (#2).

10. Disclosure control
Outputs follow the SRTR data use agreement, and tables, figures and maps stay out of the public repository until reviewed against it.

Open: the small-cell rule that applies, including flowchart boxes, risk tables and regional counts (#15).

11. Limitations to address in reporting

Small number of recipients with HIV, limiting precision and the number of matching variables.
Registry follow-up forms date events by the form, not the event.
HIV-related variables (viral load, CD4 count, antiretroviral regimen) are not in the SAF.
Residual confounding by center selection practices.
